title: 3 Ways You Should Never Vent About Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/12/05/3-ways-you-should-never-vent-about-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin acknowledges that venting to colleagues about frustrating days is normal and healthy, but warns that venting about specific students carries real risk if done carelessly. He identifies three practices to avoid: naming the student, even when it seems obvious who is meant, since it blurs the line between professional and personal conversation; venting personally by expressing dislike for the student rather than focusing on one's own feelings, since verbalized animosity solidifies and eventually surfaces in the classroom; and venting freely in hallways, offices, or lounges where anyone — including volunteers or parents — might overhear. He contrasts healthy, private venting focused on one's own emotions with the toxic habit of open, chronic complaining, which damages a teacher's reputation, relationships, and effectiveness. The piece closes with a call to choose confidants carefully and to always protect student dignity.
points: Venting to trusted colleagues about your own frustrations is healthy, but venting about specific students by name carries real risk.
Verbalizing personal dislike for a student solidifies that feeling and will eventually surface in how you treat them.
Complaining about students in hallways, offices, or lounges risks being overheard by parents or volunteers and fueling rumors.
Teachers who openly and chronically complain about students are less respected and rarely take responsibility for improving.
Healthy venting protects student dignity, focuses on your own feelings, and happens only with someone you deeply trust.
quotes: Unless you’re taking part in a professional conversation that you could or would document, you should never mention the student by name—even if it’s obvious who the student is.

When venting, keep the focus on you and your frustrations. Vent about your feelings. It’s fine to express disappointment and irritation, even anger, but avoid complaining about any student personally.
And no matter how hard you try, it’s something you can’t hide. Your dislike will reveal itself in subtle but sure ways that the student will pick up on.
It’s all too common to overhear teachers in hallways, offices, and staff lounges complaining about students by name and without a care in the world who hears them.
Teachers who openly complain about students aren’t well respected. They’re secretly avoided by most staff members.
It’s healthy when your first priority is to protect the dignity of every student in your class.
